<reason>Both sides were sharp, but B kept the debate anchored to the motion's actual question—whether indefensible men stay in places of honor—and A never contested that the men are indefensible. A's best material (the warehouse/tarp realism, the "half the job" concession extracted in pressure questions, and the "empty plinth is absolution" line) created real pressure, but B absorbed it with clean weighing: PRO's worst case ends the honor and delays the lesson, while CON's best case delivers the lesson and never ends the honor. B also turned A's cost argument (a new bronze counter-monument vs. a flatbed and signage), and when A retreated to cheap day-one measures (renaming, letterhead, plaques), B's closing exposed that the general still holds the pedestal "forever" by A's own words. A's scope-creep point landed partially (B's test did shift wording), but B's Jefferson/Colston answers were substantive enough to blunt it. B's clipped turn was a minor execution cost that lost only a final sentence. Overall B made the decision easier: position is the framing, and A's plan concedes the position.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>B's answer to A's pressure Q1 and follow-up weighing: conceding "half the job" but showing the moral half (ending honor) is the one A's plan never performs, paired with the turn that A's "taller" bronze counter-monument is costlier than the truck-and-signage A claimed cities couldn't afford.</best_rebuttal>
